title: Why Is the Milk Always at the Back of the Store?
description:
ZERO needs one carton of milk and has to walk to the far end of the supermarket for it. Who decided that? He follows the carton behind the dairy wall and finds two explanations fighting over it: a trick to make you walk past everything, and a refrigerated truck at the back door. Then he checks what the studies actually say about how much we buy without planning to.

Zero doesn't know how the world works. Yet.

Every number in this video has a source. FACT = stated by the source; ESTIMATE = our calculation or a small experiment, rounded; ILLUSTRATION = an example, not a real store's receipt.
- Grade "A" milk cooled to 7C (45F) or less and kept there (FACT): Pasteurized Milk Ordinance as adopted by states, here Maine 01-001 CMR ch. 329.
- About 3.2 hours at 25C costs a day of shelf life (ESTIMATE): Xu & Sun, Journal of Emerging Investigators, 2022, one small experiment (n=1). Ten minutes out of the cold is about an hour and a quarter of shelf life (ESTIMATE, our arithmetic on the same experiment). Real cartons vary.
- 33,248 items in the average US supermarket (FACT): FMI, The Food Retailing Industry Speaks, 2025; 45,575 supermarkets: NielsenIQ TDLinx, 2024.
- "60 to 70 percent of purchases are impulse" is an industry claim quoted in Paco Underhill, Why We Buy (1999); it is not a measurement we can check.
- 68% of items on big trips and 54% on small trips decided in the store (FACT): Inman & Winer, 1999 (via UW-Madison), 4,200 shoppers, 30,000 purchases, 14 US cities. Items, not categories.
- 18% of categories decided in the store, 1.13 of 6.4 per trip (FACT): Bell, Corsten & Knox, 2,945 trips, 21 supermarkets, Netherlands, 2006 data. Shopper-reported.
- No long trip covered all 12 aisles (FACT): Larson, Bradlow & Fader, International Journal of Research in Marketing, 2005, 8,751 cart paths in one US supermarket (data from 2001).
- Fast and efficient shoppers bought 82% less on impulse, urgent trips 53% less (FACT, an association, not a promise): Bell, Corsten & Knox.
- Milk at the back for 70 to 80 years (Burt Flickinger) and "We don't have to worry about ever breaking the cold chain" (Kevin Lang, Wegmans): NPR Planet Money, Episode 555, 2016. Their words, not independently verified.
- ZERO's $15.46 receipt is an ILLUSTRATION.
